lessons.title: Manual Cutting with Tin Snips and Shears
lessons.body:
Tin snips are your basic cutting tool for sheet metal up to about 1.2 mm thick. In Africa, you'll find three main types: straight-pattern snips for straight cuts and gentle curves, left-cut and right-cut aviation snips for tight curves, and long-handled shears for thicker gauge. Buy good quality snips with forged blades, not stamped ones â they last longer and cut cleaner. Brands like Stanley, Irwin, or local equivalents from South Africa or Kenya work well.

Start by marking your cut line with a scriber or fine marker. Clamp the sheet to your workbench using G-clamps or a vice, with the cut line just off the edge. For straight cuts, hold the snips perpendicular to the sheet and open them wide enough to bite about 5-10 mm of metal. Squeeze the handles firmly and steadily â don't force or twist, or you'll bend the metal and dull the blades. For curves, use left-cut snips for cutting clockwise and right-cut for counter-clockwise. Take small bites, especially on curves.

When cutting, wear gloves â sheet metal edges are razor sharp. Also wear safety glasses; small slivers fly off. If the snips jam, back up slightly and try again. Never cut across a previous cut or you'll damage the blades. For thicker sheets (1.5-2 mm), use a bench shear or Beverly shear instead â tin snips will struggle and ruin your hands.

Maintain your snips by oiling the pivot regularly and sharpening the blades with a fine file. Store them dry to prevent rust. In many African workshops, you'll also see 'aviation snips' with compound leverage â these cut with less effort and are great for long cuts. Practice on scrap pieces first: cut straight lines, then circles, then squares. Within an hour you'll get the feel. Remember: let the tool do the work; forcing it is the fastest way to ruin both the metal and the snips.

lessons.title: Using Bench Shears and Beverly Shears
lessons.body:
Bench shears and Beverly shears are lever-operated machines that cut sheet metal up to 3 mm thick. They are bolted to a workbench or stand. A bench shear has a straight blade and is used for straight cuts and trimming. A Beverly shear (also called a throatless shear) has a curved blade and a rotating head, allowing you to cut curves, circles, and irregular shapes. Both are common in African metal workshops because they are hand-powered, durable, and don't need electricity.

To use a bench shear: clamp it securely to a sturdy bench. The blade gap should be set to about 5% of the metal thickness â for 1 mm sheet, gap = 0.05 mm. Too wide and the metal folds; too tight and the blade wears. Mark your cut line, then insert the sheet between the blades, aligning the line with the blade edge. Pull the handle down firmly and steadily. For long cuts, feed the metal through in one smooth motion. Never cut round bar or wire â it will chip the blade.

For a Beverly shear, the process is similar but you can rotate the sheet to follow curves. The throat depth (distance from blade to frame) determines how tight a curve you can cut â typical throat is 150-200 mm. To cut a circle, drill a starter hole, insert the blade, and rotate the sheet while operating the handle. Keep the metal flat against the bed. Beverly shears are ideal for cutting auto body panels or ductwork. In Nigeria and Ghana, you'll find locally made copies of Beverly shears that work well if the blade is hardened.

Safety: always wear gloves and eye protection. Keep fingers clear of the blade â use a push stick for small pieces. Lubricate the pivot and blade with machine oil daily. Sharpen blades with a flat stone or have them professionally ground when they start leaving burrs. A well-maintained shear will last for decades. Practice on 1 mm mild steel: cut straight lines, then a 100 mm circle. You'll quickly learn the rhythm.

lessons.title: Power Shearing: Guillotine and Jump Shears
lessons.body:
When you need to cut many sheets quickly and accurately, power shears are the answer. A guillotine shear (also called a squaring shear) has a long straight blade that comes down hydraulically or mechanically. It can cut sheets up to 3-6 mm thick and 2-3 meters long. A jump shear is a smaller, foot-operated or pneumatic shear for lighter work. These machines are found in larger African metal fabrication shops, often in industrial areas of Lagos, Nairobi, or Johannesburg.

Operating a guillotine: first set the back gauge to your desired cut width. The back gauge is a stop that ensures repeatable cuts. For example, to cut 100 strips of 50 mm width from a 1 m sheet, set the back gauge to 50 mm. Clamp the sheet against the back gauge and hold it down with the hold-down foot or hydraulic clamp. Then step on the foot pedal or press the button â the blade descends and cuts. Keep hands clear of the blade! Use a squaring arm to align the sheet. For angled cuts, set the blade angle (most guillotines allow 0.5Â° to 2Â° rake). A rake angle reduces cutting force but can distort thin sheets; use 0.5Â° for thin sheets.

Jump shears are simpler: you feed the sheet and step on a pedal. They are good for cutting small pieces, notching, and trimming. Capacity is usually up to 2 mm. Always check the blade clearance: for 1 mm steel, clearance should be 0.05-0.1 mm. Too much clearance causes burrs and bending.

Safety is critical: never put your hands under the blade. Use a hand pad or push block. Wear safety glasses and gloves. Keep the machine guarded â if the guard is missing, don't use it. In many African workshops, old guillotines lack guards; retrofit a simple acrylic guard. Maintenance: oil the blades and guides daily, check hydraulic fluid monthly. A dull blade will crack the sheet instead of cutting. Sharpen or replace blades when they leave a rough edge. With practice, you can cut 100 sheets in an hour â far faster than hand shears.

lessons.title: Notching and Piercing Operations
lessons.body:
Notching is cutting a small piece out of the edge or corner of a sheet. Piercing is punching a hole without drilling. Both are common in sheet metal work for making brackets, ducting, and electrical panels. In Africa, you'll use hand notchers, nibblers, or a punch press. For light work, a hand notcher (like a Beverly shear with a corner notch attachment) works. For production, a notching machine with a V-shaped blade is used.

To notch a corner: mark the notch size, e.g., 10 mm x 10 mm. Insert the sheet into the notcher and align the marks with the blade. Pull the handle â the blade cuts out the corner. For a 90Â° notch, use a right-angle notcher. For round notches, use a rotary notcher or a hole saw. Always deburr the notch with a file. Notching is faster than drilling and cutting, and leaves a clean edge.

Piercing: use a punch and die set. A hand punch (like a Roper Whitney No. 5) can punch up to 3 mm steel. Insert the sheet between the punch and die, align the center mark, and squeeze the handle. For larger holes, use a knockout punch (e.g., Greenlee) that requires a wrench. For many holes, use a turret punch or a drill press with a hole saw. In African workshops, a common method is to drill a pilot hole then use a chassis punch. Always support the sheet to prevent distortion.

Safety: notching and piercing create sharp slugs and burrs. Wear gloves and safety glasses. Keep fingers away from the blade or punch. For punch presses, use a guard and never reach into the die area. Lubricate punches and dies with cutting oil. Check for wear â a dull punch will crack the sheet. In many shops, you'll make your own notcher from an old file and a lever â but be careful; hardened files can shatter. Better to buy a proper tool. Practice on 1 mm aluminium: notch a 10 mm corner, then punch a 6 mm hole. You'll see how these operations save time and improve accuracy.

lessons.title: Nibbling and Rotary Cutting Tools
lessons.body:
Nibbling is a cutting process that uses a small punch and die to remove metal in small bites, like a sewing machine. It is ideal for cutting curves, internal cutouts, and complex shapes in sheet metal up to 2 mm thick. A nibbler can be hand-held (electric or pneumatic) or a stand-mounted machine. Rotary cutting tools include rotary shears and circle cutters, which use rotating blades to cut circles and straight lines.

Hand-held nibblers: these look like a drill with a cutting head. You drill a starter hole (about 10 mm), insert the nibbler, and move it along your cut line. The punch moves up and down rapidly, chipping away metal. Feed speed should be slow and steady â too fast and you'll break the punch. For curves, rotate the tool as you go. In Africa, electric nibblers from Bosch or Makita are common. They cut at about 1-2 meters per minute. Always wear eye and ear protection â nibbling is noisy. Keep the cut line visible; use a guide fence for straight cuts.

Rotary shears: these have two rotating blades that cut as you push the tool. They are great for long straight cuts and gentle curves. The blades are usually hardened steel. You can also get a rotary circle cutter â a compass-like tool with a cutting wheel. Set the radius, clamp the center, and rotate the tool around. It cuts circles up to 300 mm diameter in 1 mm steel. For larger circles, use a trammel attachment.

Safety: rotary tools can grab gloves â never wear loose gloves. Use a push stick for small pieces. Unplug the tool before changing blades. Lubricate the cutting head with a few drops of oil every hour. In many African workshops, you'll see homemade rotary shears made from old gears â they work but are dangerous. Buy a proper tool. Practice on 1 mm mild steel: cut a 100 mm circle with a rotary cutter, then use a nibbler to cut an internal square. You'll find nibbling is slower than shearing but far more versatile for complex shapes.

lessons.title: Laser and Plasma Cutting Overview
lessons.body:
Laser and plasma cutting are advanced thermal cutting processes. They use a focused beam of light (laser) or a jet of ionized gas (plasma) to melt and blow away metal. In Africa, these machines are found in larger fabrication shops, often in cities like Johannesburg, Cairo, or Lagos. They are not for beginners, but you should know what they do and when to use them.

Plasma cutting: a plasma torch blows a high-temperature plasma arc through the metal. It cuts any conductive metal â steel, stainless, aluminium, copper â up to 50 mm thick (depending on power). A typical hand-held plasma cutter (e.g., Hypertherm) uses compressed air and 220V power. To cut, you clamp the work lead to the metal, put on the torch tip, press the trigger, and move at a steady speed. The cut is fast and leaves a narrow kerf (cut width). For 6 mm steel, you can cut at 1-2 meters per minute. Plasma cutting produces fumes â use ventilation. Wear a welding helmet with shade 5-8. In many African workshops, plasma cutters are used for cutting car panels, gates, and art pieces.

Laser cutting: a laser beam (CO2 or fiber) melts and vaporizes metal. It is extremely precise â kerf as small as 0.1 mm. It cuts up to 20 mm steel (fiber laser) but is usually for thin sheets (0.5-6 mm). Laser cutters are expensive and need clean power and cooling. They are used for intricate parts, signage, and automotive panels. In Africa, laser cutting services are available in major cities; you send a DXF file and get cut parts.

Safety: both processes are dangerous. Never look at the laser beam â it can blind you. Plasma produces UV radiation and hot sparks. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Never cut sealed containers or galvanized metal (toxic fumes). For beginners, focus on manual and power shearing first. But if you have access to a plasma cutter, practice on 3 mm scrap: set the amperage to 30A, air pressure to 5 bar, and cut a straight line. You'll see the speed and versatility.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness of sheet metal that tin snips can comfortably cut?
quiz.explanation: Tin snips are designed for light gauge sheet metal up to about 1.2 mm thick.

quiz.q: Which type of snips is used for cutting tight curves in a clockwise direction?
quiz.explanation: Left-cut snips are designed for cutting clockwise curves.

quiz.q: What should you do if tin snips jam while cutting?
options: B) Twist the snips to free them
C) Back up slightly and try again
D) Use a hammer to tap the blades
quiz.explanation: Backing up slightly releases the jam without damaging the blades or metal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended blade gap for a bench shear cutting 1 mm sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: The blade gap should be about 5% of the metal thickness, so 0.05 mm for 1 mm sheet.

quiz.q: What is a Beverly shear primarily used for?
options: B) Cutting curves and irregular shapes
quiz.explanation: The Beverly shear has a curved blade and rotating head for cutting curves and irregular shapes.

quiz.q: What is the throat depth of a Beverly shear?
options: A) The length of the handle
B) The distance from blade to frame
C) The thickness of the blade
D) The width of the cut
quiz.explanation: Throat depth is the distance from the blade to the frame, determining the maximum curve size.

quiz.q: On a guillotine shear, what is the back gauge used for?
options: B) To set repeatable cut widths
quiz.explanation: The back gauge is a stop that ensures each cut is the same width.

quiz.q: What rake angle is recommended for cutting thin sheets on a guillotine?
quiz.explanation: A small rake angle of 0.5Â° reduces distortion on thin sheets.

quiz.q: What is the typical capacity of a jump shear?
quiz.explanation: Jump shears are light-duty and typically cut up to 2 mm thick sheet metal.

quiz.q: What safety device should never be missing on a guillotine shear?
quiz.explanation: A guard protects hands from the descending blade and is essential for safety.

quiz.q: What is notching?
options: A) Cutting a hole in the middle of a sheet
B) Cutting a small piece out of the edge or corner
quiz.explanation: Notching removes a small section from the edge or corner of a sheet.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for punching a 6 mm hole in 3 mm steel?
quiz.explanation: A hand punch like a Roper Whitney No. 5 can punch holes up to 3 mm thick.

quiz.q: What is a common method for making a large hole in sheet metal in African workshops?
options: A) Using a hammer and chisel
B) Drilling a pilot hole then using a chassis punch
quiz.explanation: Drilling a pilot hole then using a chassis punch is a common and effective method.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a homemade notcher from an old file?
options: C) It leaves a rough edge
quiz.explanation: Hardened files are brittle and can shatter, causing injury.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness of sheet metal that a hand-held nibbler can typically cut?
quiz.explanation: Hand-held nibblers are designed for sheet metal up to about 2 mm thick.

quiz.q: What should you do before inserting a nibbler into a sheet?
quiz.explanation: A starter hole allows the nibbler's punch to enter the metal.

quiz.q: What is a rotary circle cutter used for?
quiz.explanation: A rotary circle cutter is designed to cut circles by rotating around a center point.

quiz.q: Why should you never wear loose gloves when using rotary cutting tools?
options: A) They can get caught and pull your hand in
quiz.explanation: Loose gloves can be grabbed by the rotating blades, pulling your hand into the tool.

quiz.q: What is the typical kerf width of a plasma cutter?
quiz.explanation: Plasma cutting leaves a kerf of about 1-2 mm, depending on the nozzle and material.

quiz.q: Which gas is commonly used in hand-held plasma cutters?
quiz.explanation: Compressed air is the most common gas for hand-held plasma cutters in workshops.

quiz.q: What shade of welding helmet is recommended for plasma cutting?
quiz.explanation: Shade 5-8 protects eyes from the bright plasma arc and UV radiation.

quiz.q: What is the maximum thickness that a fiber laser can typically cut?
quiz.explanation: Fiber lasers can cut up to about 20 mm steel, though usually for thinner sheets.

quiz.q: Why is laser cutting not common in small African workshops?
options: B) It requires expensive equipment and clean power
quiz.explanation: Laser cutters are expensive and need stable power and cooling, limiting their use in small workshops.

quiz.q: What should you never cut with a plasma cutter?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized metal releases toxic fumes when cut with plasma.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a squaring arm on a guillotine shear?
options: B) To align the sheet at 90 degrees
quiz.explanation: A squaring arm helps align the sheet perpendicular to the blade for square cuts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance for a jump shear cutting 1 mm steel?
quiz.explanation: Clearance of 0.05-0.1 mm is typical for 1 mm steel to avoid burrs and bending.

quiz.q: What is a common hand tool for deburring after notching?
quiz.explanation: A file is used to remove sharp burrs after notching.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of a nibbler over a hand shear for cutting internal cutouts?
options: B) It can start from a drilled hole
quiz.explanation: A nibbler can start from a drilled hole and cut internal shapes, which hand shears cannot do easily.

quiz.q: What is the typical cutting speed of a hand-held nibbler?
quiz.explanation: Hand-held nibblers typically cut at 1-2 meters per minute.

quiz.q: What should you do before changing blades on a rotary shear?
quiz.explanation: Always unplug power tools before changing blades to prevent accidental start.
